title: Why money comes in coins and notes
description: Coins rattle, notes fold. Money comes in two forms because the two materials solve opposite problems: small amounts need something nearly indestructible, large amounts need something light.

body.heading: Coins: built to outlive us
paragraphs: A coin may pass through thousands of hands over decades, so coins are struck from hard metal alloys that shrug off pockets, tills and washing machines. Minting a coin costs more than printing a note of the same value — but spread over thirty years of use, the coin is far cheaper per year.
That is also why coins stay small in value: a heavy purse of high-value coins would be secure but miserable to carry, and a lost coin purse loses real metal-era value with every step.

body.heading: Notes: light, printable, replaceable
paragraphs: Notes — today usually printed on polymer or cotton paper — carry large values in almost no weight, and their surfaces hold the detailed artwork, threads and watermarks that make forgery hard. Their weakness is wear: notes tear and soil, and are withdrawn and replaced after a few years.

So the system splits the job: coins for the small, constant, hard-wearing traffic of daily life; notes for the larger sums that move less often. Two forms, one wallet, each doing what its material does best.

takeaway: Coins are expensive to make but last for decades of daily use; notes are light and hard to forge but wear out — money's two forms split the job by material.
